title: Das Wasser des Lebens
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 97. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 97, a three-brothers quest built on the pattern of two proud elders and one courteous youngest. A dying king’s sons set out for the water of life; the eldest two answer a dwarf on the road with contempt and are cursed to be wedged fast between two mountains, while the youngest answers politely and is given what he needs to win through an enchanted castle — an iron rod, two loaves for its lions, and a midnight deadline that costs him a sliver of his heel on the way out. He frees his brothers, feeds and arms three starving kingdoms along the way home, and is nearly destroyed by those same brothers, who swap his water for seawater and accuse him of trying to poison their father — until a bride’s golden road and a huntsman’s mercy set things right.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der war krank, und niemand glaubte daß er mit dem Leben davon käme.
sentences.l: There was once a king, he was sick, and nobody believed that he would come away with his life.
sentences.i: There was once a king who was sick, and no one believed he would come through it alive.
sentences.n: “der war krank” — the relative pronoun der is carried on as a demonstrative and the clause runs like a main clause: “that one was sick.” “mit dem Leben davonkommen” is the fixed expression for getting off with one’s life. käme is the subjunctive of reported belief; daß is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: Er hatte aber drei Söhne, die waren darüber betrübt, giengen hinunter in den Schloßgarten und weinten.
sentences.l: He had, however, three sons, they were grieved over it, went down into the castle-garden and wept.
sentences.i: But he had three sons, who were grieved at it; they went down into the castle garden and wept.
sentences.n: aber stands second by the V2 habit where English wants “but” first. Again “die waren” — a relative pronoun continued as a demonstrative, so the sentence simply runs on. giengen is the 1857 spelling of gingen.

sentences.t: Da begegnete ihnen ein alter Mann, der fragte sie nach ihrem Kummer.
sentences.l: There met them an old man, he asked them after their sorrow.
sentences.i: There an old man met them, who asked them what their trouble was.
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative, so ihnen is the party met. “fragen nach” = to ask after, ask about. Kummer is grief, trouble, the weight on the heart.

sentences.t: Sie sagten ihm ihr Vater wäre so krank, daß er wohl sterben würde, denn es wollte ihm nichts helfen.
sentences.l: They said to him their father was so sick that he would surely die, for nothing wanted to help him.
sentences.i: They told him their father was so sick that he would surely die, for nothing would do him any good.
sentences.n: wäre and würde are the subjunctive of reported speech: the tale gives the sons’ words without quoting them, and English marks this only by “they said.” wohl here is “no doubt, surely,” not “well.” “es wollte ihm nichts helfen” uses wollen of the stubbornness of things: nothing would help.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Alte „ich weiß noch ein Mittel, das ist das Wasser des Lebens, wenn er davon trinkt, so wird er wieder gesund: es ist aber schwer zu finden.“
sentences.l: Then spoke the old man “I know yet one remedy, that is the water of life, if he drinks of it, then he becomes well again: but it is hard to find.”
sentences.i: Then the old man said: “I know of one remedy still — it is the water of life; if he drinks of it he will grow well again, but it is hard to find.”
sentences.n: Mittel is a means, here a remedy. “davon trinken” = to drink of it, davon standing for the water. The answering so after a wenn-clause is “then.” der Alte is an adjective used as a noun, the old man. sprach is this tale’s ordinary verb of saying, a step more formal than sagte.

sentences.t: Der älteste sagte „ich will es schon finden,“ gieng zum kranken König und bat ihn er möchte ihm erlauben auszuziehen um das Wasser des Lebens zu suchen, denn das könnte ihn allein heilen.
sentences.l: The eldest said “I will find it right enough,” went to the sick king and begged him he might allow him to set out in order to seek the water of life, for that alone could heal him.
sentences.i: The eldest said: “I shall find it, never fear,” and went to the sick king and begged him to allow him to set out and look for the water of life, for that alone could cure him.
sentences.n: schon in a promise is the little word of confidence — I shall find it, never doubt it; it is not “already” here. From er möchte the sentence turns into reported speech in the subjunctive (möchte, könnte). ausziehen is to set out, march out, said of soldiers and of sons leaving home.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sprach der König, „die Gefahr dabei ist zu groß, lieber will ich sterben.“
sentences.l: “No,” spoke the king, “the danger in it is too great, rather will I die.”
sentences.i: “No,” said the king, “the danger of it is too great; I would rather die.”
sentences.n: dabei = with it, in the doing of it. lieber is the comparative of gern, so wollen with lieber gives “would rather”; fronting it drives the verb ahead of the subject.

sentences.t: Er bat aber so lange, bis der König einwilligte.
sentences.l: He begged, however, so long, until the king consented.
sentences.i: But he begged so long that the king consented at last.
sentences.n: “so lange, bis …” states the duration where English says “so long that.” einwilligen, to consent, is separable — willigte … ein in a main clause, but held together here at the end of its own clause.

sentences.t: Der Prinz dachte in seinem Herzen „bringe ich das Wasser, so bin ich meinem Vater der liebste und erbe das Reich.“
sentences.l: The prince thought in his heart “bring I the water, then am I my father’s dearest and inherit the kingdom.”
sentences.i: The prince thought in his heart: “If I bring the water, I shall be my father’s favourite and inherit the kingdom.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first — “bringe ich das Wasser” — and the answering clause opens with so. “meinem Vater der liebste” puts the person concerned in the dative: the dearest to my father. Reich is a kingdom, a realm.

sentences.t: Also machte er sich auf, und als er eine Zeitlang fortgeritten war, stand da ein Zwerg auf dem Wege, der rief ihn an und sprach „wo hinaus so geschwind?“
sentences.l: So he set himself out, and when he had ridden away a while, there stood a dwarf on the road, he called to him and spoke “where out so fast?”
sentences.i: So he set out; and when he had ridden on for a while, a dwarf stood there in the road, who called to him and said: “where away so fast?”
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” = to set out, with the prefix auf landing at the end. Also is “so, thus,” never English “also.” anrufen is to call out to someone: rief … an. “wo hinaus?” is an old elliptical question — where out, i.e. where are you off to — with no verb at all.

sentences.t: „Dummer Knirps,“ sagte der Prinz ganz stolz, „das brauchst du nicht zu wissen“ und ritt weiter.
sentences.l: “Stupid little runt,” said the prince quite proudly, “that you need not know” and rode further.
sentences.i: “Stupid little runt,” said the prince very proudly, “you have no need to know that” — and rode on.
sentences.n: Knirps is a very small person said contemptuously: a shrimp, a runt. “brauchen … zu” with nicht means “need not.” Fronting das gives it the emphasis, and the verb keeps its second place.

sentences.t: Das kleine Männchen aber war zornig geworden und hatte einen bösen Wunsch gethan.
sentences.l: The little manikin, however, had grown angry and had done an evil wish.
sentences.i: But the little man had grown angry, and had wished an evil wish.
sentences.n: Männchen is the diminutive of Mann. “einen Wunsch thun” = to make a wish; thun is the 1857 spelling of tun, gethan of getan. böse covers both “evil” and “angry,” and the wish is a curse.

sentences.t: Der Prinz gerieth bald hernach in eine Bergschlucht, und je weiter er ritt, je enger thaten sich die Berge zusammen, und endlich ward der Weg so eng, daß er keinen Schritt weiter konnte;
sentences.l: The prince got soon thereafter into a mountain-gorge, and the further he rode, the narrower the mountains drew themselves together, and at last the way became so narrow that he could not [go] a step further;
sentences.i: Soon after, the prince got into a mountain gorge; and the further he rode the closer the mountains drew together, until at last the way became so narrow that he could not go a step further;
sentences.n: gerathen (modern geraten) is to come into a place or a state without meaning to. “je … je …” is the older form of “je … desto”: the further, the narrower. konnte stands with no verb of motion at all — a modal does the work alone in German — so the English supplies [go]; that bracket is ours, not the Grimms’. ward is the old past of werden.

sentences.t: es war nicht möglich das Pferd zu wenden oder aus dem Sattel zu steigen, und er saß da wie eingesperrt.
sentences.l: it was not possible to turn the horse or to climb out of the saddle, and he sat there as if locked in.
sentences.i: it was not possible to turn the horse or to get out of the saddle, and he sat there as though he were shut up.
sentences.n: wenden is to turn a thing about. “wie eingesperrt” — like [one] shut in; einsperren is to lock up, and the bare participle stands as the whole comparison.

sentences.t: Der kranke König wartete lange Zeit auf ihn, aber er kam nicht.
sentences.l: The sick king waited a long time for him, but he did not come.
sentences.n: “warten auf” takes the accusative for the one waited for. “lange Zeit” is a bare accusative of duration, with no preposition where English wants “for.”

sentences.t: Da sagte der zweite Sohn „Vater, laßt mich ausziehen und das Wasser suchen,“ und dachte bei sich „ist mein Bruder todt, so fällt das Reich mir zu.“
sentences.l: Then said the second son “Father, let me set out and seek the water,” and thought to himself “is my brother dead, then the kingdom falls to me.”
sentences.i: Then the second son said: “Father, let me set out and look for the water” — and thought to himself: “if my brother is dead, the kingdom falls to me.”
sentences.n: laßt is the plural imperative: the son says ihr to his father, the ordinary respectful plural of the tales. “bei sich denken” = to think to oneself. Another conditional without wenn, the verb standing first: “ist mein Bruder todt.” zufallen, to fall to someone as his share, is separable: fällt … zu. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Der König wollt ihn anfangs auch nicht ziehen lassen, endlich gab er nach.
sentences.l: The king would not let him go at first either, at last he gave way.
sentences.i: At first the king would not let him go either; at last he gave in.
sentences.n: wollt is wollte with the ending clipped, as speech does. “ziehen lassen” = to let go, let march off. “auch nicht” = not … either. nachgeben, to give in, is separable: gab … nach.

sentences.t: Der Prinz zog also auf demselben Weg fort, den sein Bruder eingeschlagen hatte, und begegnete auch dem Zwerg, der ihn anhielt und fragte wohin er so eilig wollte.
sentences.l: The prince set off then on the same road that his brother had taken, and met the dwarf too, who stopped him and asked where he wanted [to go] so hurriedly.
sentences.i: So the prince rode off along the same road his brother had taken, and he too met the dwarf, who stopped him and asked where he was going in such haste.
sentences.n: “einen Weg einschlagen” is the set phrase for taking a road, striking into it. wollte again stands with no infinitive of motion — where he wanted [to go]; the bracket is ours. fortziehen is separable: zog … fort.

sentences.t: „Kleiner Knirps,“ sagte der Prinz, „das brauchst du nicht zu wissen“ und ritt fort ohne sich weiter umzusehen.
sentences.l: “Little runt,” said the prince, “that you need not know” and rode off without looking about him further.
sentences.i: “Little runt,” said the prince, “you have no need to know that” — and rode off without so much as looking round.
sentences.n: “sich umsehen” = to look about one. With ohne … zu the zu goes inside the separable verb: umzusehen. The second brother repeats the first almost word for word; the tales mark a pattern by repeating it rather than remarking on it.

sentences.t: Aber der Zwerg verwünschte ihn, und er gerieth wie der andere in eine Bergschlucht und konnte nicht vorwärts und rückwärts.
sentences.l: But the dwarf cursed him, and he got like the other into a mountain-gorge and could not forwards and backwards.
sentences.i: But the dwarf laid a curse on him, and like the other he got into a mountain gorge and could go neither forward nor back.
sentences.n: verwünschen is to curse, to lay a spell on — the same verb used later of the enchanted castle and its princes. Again a modal with no verb of motion: “konnte nicht vorwärts und rückwärts.”

sentences.t: So gehts aber den Hochmüthigen.
sentences.l: So it goes, however, for the haughty.
sentences.i: But so it goes with the haughty.
sentences.n: gehts = geht es. “es geht jemandem so” — things go thus for someone, the person standing in the dative: den Hochmüthigen. hochmüthig (modern hochmütig) is high-minded in the bad sense, overweening; the adjective is used as a plural noun. The narrator steps forward for one line to point the moral, then withdraws.

sentences.t: Als auch der zweite Sohn ausblieb, so erbot sich der jüngste auszuziehen und das Wasser zu holen, und der König mußte ihn endlich ziehen lassen.
sentences.l: When the second son too stayed away, then the youngest offered himself to set out and fetch the water, and the king had to let him go at last.
sentences.i: When the second son too failed to come back, the youngest offered to set out and fetch the water, and at last the king had to let him go.
sentences.n: ausbleiben is to stay away, to fail to appear. “sich erbieten” = to offer oneself, to volunteer. The main clause after an als-clause opens with so, which English simply leaves out.

sentences.t: Als er dem Zwerg begegnete, und dieser fragte wohin er so eilig wolle, so hielt er an, gab ihm Rede und Antwort und sagte „ich suche das Wasser des Lebens, denn mein Vater ist sterbenskrank.“
sentences.l: When he met the dwarf, and this one asked where he wanted [to go] so hurriedly, then he stopped, gave him speech and answer and said “I seek the water of life, for my father is deathly sick.”
sentences.i: When he met the dwarf, and the dwarf asked where he was going in such haste, he stopped, gave him a proper answer, and said: “I am looking for the water of life, for my father is sick unto death.”
sentences.n: dieser, “this one,” points back to the dwarf and keeps the two men apart without naming either. “Rede und Antwort geben” is a fixed pair: to answer properly, to give an account of oneself — the courtesy the two elder brothers refused. wolle is the subjunctive of the reported question. As at the dwarf’s first meeting, wollte/wolle stands with no infinitive of motion, so the English supplies [to go]; that bracket is ours, not the Grimms’. sterbenskrank is sick to the point of dying.

sentences.t: „Weißt du auch wo das zu finden ist?“
sentences.l: “Do you know too where that is to be found?”
sentences.i: “And do you know where it is to be found?”
sentences.n: auch in a question is not “also” but a probing turn: do you actually know? “zu finden ist” is sein + zu + infinitive, which carries a passive sense of possibility — is to be found, can be found.

sentences.t: „Nein“ sagte der Prinz.
sentences.l: “No” said the prince.
sentences.n: The 1857 text sets no comma between the speech and sagte here; the edition punctuates dialogue lightly and unevenly, and it is left exactly as printed.

sentences.t: „Weil du dich betragen hast, wie sichs geziemt, nicht übermüthig wie deine falschen Brüder, so will ich dir Auskunft geben und dir sagen wie du zu dem Wasser des Lebens gelangst.
sentences.l: “Because you have borne yourself as is fitting, not overweening like your false brothers, so I will give you information and tell you how you get to the water of life.
sentences.i: “Because you have behaved as is fitting, and not haughtily like your false brothers, I will tell you what you need to know, and say how you may reach the water of life.
sentences.n: “sich betragen” = to conduct oneself. sichs = sich es, and “wie sichs geziemt” = as is seemly, as it befits one; geziemen is old and formal. Auskunft is information, directions. gelangen is to reach, to arrive at, a shade more formal than kommen.

sentences.t: Es quillt aus einem Brunnen in dem Hofe eines verwünschten Schlosses, aber du dringst nicht hinein, wenn ich dir nicht eine eiserne Ruthe gebe und zwei Laiberchen Brot.
sentences.l: It wells out of a well in the courtyard of an enchanted castle, but you do not press in, if I do not give you an iron rod and two little loaves of bread.
sentences.i: It springs from a well in the courtyard of an enchanted castle; but you will not get in unless I give you an iron rod and two little loaves of bread.
sentences.n: quellen is to well up, to spring — the verb behind Quelle, a spring. verwünscht is “under a spell,” enchanted rather than damned. dringen is to press, to force one’s way. Laiberchen is a diminutive of Laib, a loaf. German states both halves in the present where English wants a future and an “unless.”

sentences.t: Mit der Ruthe schlag dreimal an das eiserne Thor des Schlosses, so wird es aufspringen:
sentences.l: With the rod strike three times on the iron gate of the castle, then it will spring open:
sentences.i: Strike the castle’s iron gate three times with the rod, and it will fly open:
sentences.n: schlag is the du-imperative in its old bare form, without an -e. “anschlagen an” = to strike against. aufspringen is to spring open, said of a door. Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor.

sentences.t: inwendig liegen zwei Löwen, die den Rachen aufsperren, wenn du aber jedem ein Brot hinein wirfst, so werden sie still
sentences.l: inside lie two lions, which tear open their jaws, but if you throw each one a bread in, then they become quiet
sentences.i: inside lie two lions with their jaws gaping wide; but if you throw each of them a loaf, they will grow quiet
sentences.n: inwendig = within, inside. der Rachen is the throat and gape of a beast, and aufsperren is to force wide open. hinein is “in there, away from the speaker,” and the 1857 text prints it as a word of its own rather than joined to wirfst.

sentences.t: und dann eile dich und hol von dem Wasser des Lebens bevor es zwölf schlägt, sonst schlägt das Thor wieder zu und du bist eingesperrt.“
sentences.l: and then hurry yourself and fetch of the water of life before it strikes twelve, else the gate strikes to again and you are locked in.”
sentences.i: and then make haste and fetch some of the water of life before it strikes twelve, or the gate will slam shut again and you will be shut in.”
sentences.n: “sich eilen” is reflexive: hurry yourself. hol is the clipped imperative of holen. “von dem Wasser” is partitive — some of the water. “es schlägt zwölf” has the impersonal es of a striking clock. zuschlagen, to slam shut, is separable: schlägt … zu.

sentences.t: Der Prinz dankte ihm, nahm die Ruthe und das Brot, und machte sich auf den Weg.
sentences.l: The prince thanked him, took the rod and the bread, and made himself on the way.
sentences.i: The prince thanked him, took the rod and the bread, and set out on his way.
sentences.n: danken takes the dative: ihm. “sich auf den Weg machen” is the fixed phrase for setting out on a journey.

sentences.t: Und als er anlangte, war alles so, wie der Zwerg gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: And when he arrived, everything was so, as the dwarf had said.
sentences.i: And when he arrived, everything was just as the dwarf had said.
sentences.n: anlangen is to arrive, an older cousin of ankommen. “so … wie” pairs off: thus … as.

sentences.t: Das Thor sprang beim dritten Ruthenschlag auf, und als er die Löwen mit dem Brot gesänftigt hatte, trat er in das Schloß und kam in einen großen schönen Saal:
sentences.l: The gate sprang open at the third rod-stroke, and when he had soothed the lions with the bread, he stepped into the castle and came into a great fine hall:
sentences.i: At the third stroke of the rod the gate flew open; and when he had quieted the lions with the bread, he stepped into the castle and came into a great fine hall:
sentences.n: Ruthenschlag is a compound made on the spot: rod-stroke. sänftigen is an old verb, to make gentle (sanft), to soothe. Saal is a great room, a hall of state.

sentences.t: darin saßen verwünschte Prinzen, denen zog er die Ringe vom Finger, dann lag da ein Schwert und ein Brot, das nahm er weg.
sentences.l: in it sat enchanted princes, from those he drew the rings off the finger, then there lay a sword and a bread, that he took away.
sentences.i: in it sat princes under a spell; he drew the rings from their fingers; then there lay a sword and a loaf, and those he took away.
sentences.n: “denen zog er die Ringe vom Finger” is the dative of possession: the owner of the finger stands in the dative (denen), and German says “the finger” where English says “their.” The relative denen is fronted, hooking the clause onto what came before. The tale does not say why he takes the rings; it simply reports it.

sentences.t: Und weiter kam er in ein Zimmer, darin stand eine schöne Jungfrau, die freute sich, als sie ihn sah, küßte ihn und sagte er hätte sie erlöst, und sollte ihr ganzes Reich haben, und wenn er in einem Jahr wieder käme, so sollte ihre Hochzeit gefeiert werden.
sentences.l: And further he came into a chamber, in it stood a beautiful maiden, she rejoiced when she saw him, kissed him and said he had released her, and should have her whole kingdom, and if he came again in a year, then their wedding should be celebrated.
sentences.i: And going further he came into a chamber where a beautiful maiden stood; she rejoiced when she saw him, kissed him, and said that he had set her free and should have her whole kingdom, and that if he came again within a year their wedding should be held.
sentences.n: erlösen is this book’s word for breaking a spell: to release, to set free. From er hätte onward everything is subjunctive of reported speech — hätte, sollte, käme — so her words are given without being quoted. “sich freuen” = to be glad.

sentences.t: Dann sagte sie ihm auch, wo der Brunnen wäre mit dem Lebenswasser, er müßte sich aber eilen und daraus schöpfen eh es zwölf schlüge.
sentences.l: Then she told him also where the well was with the water-of-life, but he must hurry himself and draw from it before it struck twelve.
sentences.i: Then she told him too where the well with the water of life stood, but that he must make haste and draw from it before the clock struck twelve.
sentences.n: Lebenswasser packs “das Wasser des Lebens” into a single word. schöpfen is to draw water with a vessel. eh is the clipped ehe, before. wäre, müßte and schlüge are all reported-speech subjunctives.

sentences.t: Da gieng er weiter und kam endlich in ein Zimmer, wo ein schönes frischgedecktes Bett stand, und weil er müde war, wollt er erst ein wenig ausruhen.
sentences.l: Then he went further and came at last into a chamber where a fine freshly-made bed stood, and because he was tired, he wanted first to rest a little.
sentences.i: Then he went on, and came at last into a room where a fine bed stood freshly made; and because he was tired, he thought he would rest a little first.
sentences.n: frischgedeckt is literally freshly covered, said of a bed newly made up with clean linen. erst is “first, before anything else.” wollt is the clipped wollte.

sentences.t: Also legte er sich und schlief ein: als er erwachte, schlug es drei Viertel auf zwölf.
sentences.l: So he laid himself down and fell asleep: when he awoke, it struck three quarters onto twelve.
sentences.i: So he lay down and fell asleep; when he awoke, the clock struck a quarter to twelve.
sentences.n: “sich legen” = to lie down. einschlafen is separable: schlief … ein. “drei Viertel auf zwölf” is the old way of telling the hour in the south and centre of Germany — three quarters of the way to twelve, that is, a quarter to twelve.

sentences.t: Da sprang er ganz erschrocken auf, lief zu dem Brunnen und schöpfte daraus mit einem Becher, der daneben stand, und eilte daß er fortkam.
sentences.l: Then he sprang up quite frightened, ran to the well and drew from it with a cup that stood beside it, and hurried that he got away.
sentences.i: Then he sprang up in a fright, ran to the well and drew from it with a cup that stood beside it, and hurried to be gone.
sentences.n: erschrocken is the participle of erschrecken doing duty as a description of him: startled, in a fright. aufspringen is separable: sprang … auf. “eilte daß er fortkam” is a daß-clause of purpose where English prefers an infinitive.

sentences.t: Wie er eben zum eisernen Thor hinaus gieng, da schlugs zwölf, und das Thor schlug so heftig zu, daß es ihm noch ein Stück von der Ferse wegnahm.
sentences.l: As he was just going out through the iron gate, there it struck twelve, and the gate slammed to so violently that it took away from him yet a piece of the heel.
sentences.i: Just as he was going out through the iron gate, twelve struck, and the gate slammed to so violently that it carried away a piece of his heel.
sentences.n: wie here is “as, just as,” in time; eben is “just at that moment.” schlugs = schlug es. Once more the dative of possession: ihm carries the owner of the heel where English says “his heel.” The tale reports the injury without softening it.

sentences.t: Er aber war froh daß er das Wasser des Lebens erlangt hatte, gieng heimwärts und kam wieder an dem Zwerg vorbei.
sentences.l: He, however, was glad that he had obtained the water of life, went homewards and came past the dwarf again.
sentences.i: But he was glad that he had won the water of life; he went homewards, and came past the dwarf again.
sentences.n: erlangen is to obtain, to attain to a thing. “vorbeikommen an” = to come past something, the prefix vorbei waiting at the end: kam … vorbei. heimwärts keeps the old ending English still has in “homewards.”

sentences.t: Als dieser das Schwert und das Brot sah, sprach er „damit hast du großes Gut gewonnen, mit dem Schwert kannst du ganze Heere schlagen, das Brot aber wird niemals all.“
sentences.l: When this one saw the sword and the bread, he spoke “with that you have won great goods, with the sword you can beat whole armies, but the bread never becomes all.”
sentences.i: When the dwarf saw the sword and the bread, he said: “with those you have won great riches; with the sword you can beat whole armies, and the bread will never be used up.”
sentences.n: Gut is goods, property, what a man is worth. “all werden” is an old phrase, still alive in dialect, for a stock coming to an end: the bread never runs out. Heer is an army, plural Heere.

sentences.t: Der Prinz wollte ohne seine Brüder nicht zu dem Vater nach Haus kommen und sprach „lieber Zwerg, kannst du mir nicht sagen, wo meine zwei Brüder sind? sie sind früher als ich nach dem Wasser des Lebens ausgezogen und sind nicht wiedergekommen.“
sentences.l: The prince would not come home to the father without his brothers and spoke “dear dwarf, can you not tell me where my two brothers are? they set out earlier than I after the water of life and have not come back again.”
sentences.i: The prince did not want to come home to his father without his brothers, and said: “dear dwarf, can you not tell me where my two brothers are? they set out for the water of life before I did, and have not come back.”
sentences.n: “nach Haus kommen” = to come home. The question mark inside the speech is followed by a small letter — the 1857 edition does this regularly, and it stands as printed. “ausziehen nach” is to set out after a thing, to go in quest of it.

sentences.t: „Zwischen zwei Bergen stecken sie eingeschlossen,“ sprach der Zwerg, „dahin habe ich sie verwünscht, weil sie so übermüthig waren.“
sentences.l: “Between two mountains they stick shut in,” spoke the dwarf, “thither have I cursed them, because they were so overweening.”
sentences.i: “They are stuck fast between two mountains,” said the dwarf; “that is where my curse sent them, because they were so haughty.”
sentences.n: stecken is to be stuck fast, wedged. “dahin verwünschen” — to curse someone to a place, to send him there by a spell; dahin stands first and drives the verb ahead of the subject. übermüthig (modern übermütig) is overweening, riding high.

sentences.t: Da bat der Prinz so lange, bis der Zwerg sie wieder los ließ, aber er warnte ihn und sprach „hüte dich vor ihnen, sie haben ein böses Herz.“
sentences.l: Then the prince begged so long, until the dwarf let them loose again, but he warned him and spoke “guard yourself against them, they have an evil heart.”
sentences.i: Then the prince begged so long that the dwarf let them go again; but he warned him and said: “be on your guard against them, they have an evil heart.”
sentences.n: “los lassen” = to let loose, to release; the 1857 text prints it as two words. “sich hüten vor” = to be on one’s guard against, the reflexive in the accusative: hüte dich. The two brothers get one Herz between them, as German idiom prefers.

sentences.t: Als seine Brüder kamen, freute er sich und erzählte ihnen wie es ihm ergangen wäre, daß er das Wasser des Lebens gefunden und einen Becher voll mitgenommen und eine schöne Prinzessin erlöst hätte, die wollte ein Jahr lang auf ihn warten, dann sollte Hochzeit gehalten werden, und er bekäme ein großes Reich.
sentences.l: When his brothers came, he was glad and told them how it had gone with him, that he had found the water of life and taken a cup full with him and released a beautiful princess, she would wait a year long for him, then a wedding should be held, and he would get a great kingdom.
sentences.i: When his brothers came, he rejoiced, and told them how it had gone with him: that he had found the water of life and taken a cupful away with him, and set free a beautiful princess who would wait a year for him, and then the wedding should be held, and he would have a great kingdom.
sentences.n: “es ist mir so ergangen” = things went thus with me, the person in the dative: ihm. wäre, hätte, bekäme are the reported-speech subjunctives running through the whole sentence. “ein Jahr lang” = for a whole year, with lang following its noun.

sentences.t: Danach ritten sie zusammen fort und geriethen in ein Land, wo Hunger und Krieg war, und der König glaubte schon er müßte verderben, so groß war die Noth.
sentences.l: After that they rode away together and got into a land where hunger and war were, and the king already believed he must perish, so great was the need.
sentences.i: After that they rode away together, and came into a land where there was famine and war; and the king already believed he must be ruined, so great was the distress.
sentences.n: gerathen again for coming somewhere unplanned. verderben is to perish, to be ruined. Noth (modern Not) is want, distress, dire straits, and covers hunger and danger together. Fronting “so groß” throws the verb before its subject.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Prinz zu ihm und gab ihm das Brot, womit er sein ganzes Reich speiste und sättigte:
sentences.l: Then the prince went to him and gave him the bread, with which he fed and satisfied his whole kingdom:
sentences.i: Then the prince went to him and gave him the bread, with which he fed his whole kingdom and satisfied it:
sentences.n: womit = with which; German binds the preposition and the pronoun into one word. speisen is to feed; sättigen is to fill to satisfaction, from satt, full.

sentences.t: und dann gab ihm der Prinz auch das Schwert, damit schlug er die Heere seiner Feinde und konnte nun in Ruhe und Frieden leben.
sentences.l: and then the prince gave him the sword too, with it he beat the armies of his enemies and could now live in rest and peace.
sentences.i: and then the prince gave him the sword as well, and with it he beat the armies of his enemies, and could now live in rest and peace.
sentences.n: damit is “with that,” pointing back to the sword; standing first it drives the verb ahead of the subject. “in Ruhe und Frieden” is a fixed pair, like the English “in peace and quiet.”

sentences.t: Da nahm der Prinz sein Brot und Schwert wieder zurück, und die drei Brüder ritten weiter.
sentences.l: Then the prince took his bread and sword back again, and the three brothers rode further.
sentences.i: Then the prince took back his bread and sword, and the three brothers rode on.
sentences.n: zurücknehmen is separable — nahm … zurück — with wieder tucked in before the prefix.

sentences.t: Sie kamen aber noch in zwei Länder, wo Hunger und Krieg herrschten, und da gab der Prinz den Königen jedesmal sein Brot und Schwert, und hatte nun drei Reiche gerettet.
sentences.l: But they came into two more lands where hunger and war reigned, and there the prince gave the kings each time his bread and sword, and had now saved three kingdoms.
sentences.i: But they came into two more lands where famine and war were raging, and each time the prince gave the kings his bread and sword; and so he had now saved three kingdoms.
sentences.n: herrschen is to rule, to hold sway — said of a lord and equally of a famine. jedesmal = each time. Länder is the plural of Land, with the umlaut.

sentences.t: Und danach setzten sie sich auf ein Schiff, und fuhren übers Meer.
sentences.l: And after that they set themselves on a ship, and travelled over the sea.
sentences.i: And after that they went aboard a ship, and sailed over the sea.
sentences.n: “sich auf ein Schiff setzen” = to take ship, to go aboard. fahren is the general verb for travelling by any conveyance; übers = über das.

sentences.t: Während der Fahrt da sprachen die beiden ältesten unter sich „der jüngste hat das Wasser des Lebens gefunden und wir nicht, dafür wird ihm unser Vater das Reich geben, das uns gebührt, und er wird unser Glück wegnehmen.“
sentences.l: During the voyage there the two eldest spoke among themselves “the youngest has found the water of life and we not, for that our father will give him the kingdom that is due to us, and he will take away our fortune.”
sentences.i: During the voyage the two eldest said to one another: “the youngest has found the water of life and we have not; for that our father will give him the kingdom which is our due, and he will take our fortune away from us.”
sentences.n: The da after the time phrase is a resumptive “then, there” that German likes and English drops. “unter sich” = among themselves. gebühren is to be due to someone by right, the person in the dative: uns. Glück is both luck and the good fortune a man has coming to him.

sentences.t: Da wurden sie rachsüchtig und verabredeten mit einander daß sie ihn verderben wollten.
sentences.l: Then they became vengeful and agreed with one another that they would ruin him.
sentences.i: Then they grew vengeful, and agreed together that they would destroy him.
sentences.n: rachsüchtig is Rache (revenge) with -süchtig (craving, addicted): craving revenge. “sich verabreden” is to settle a thing between them; the 1857 text prints mit einander apart. verderben is transitive here: to ruin, to do for someone.

sentences.t: Sie warteten bis er einmal fest eingeschlafen war, da gossen sie das Wasser des Lebens aus dem Becher und nahmen es für sich, ihm aber gossen sie bitteres Meerwasser hinein.
sentences.l: They waited until he had once fallen fast asleep, then they poured the water of life out of the cup and took it for themselves, but to him they poured bitter sea-water in.
sentences.i: They waited until he had fallen fast asleep, and then poured the water of life out of the cup and kept it for themselves, and poured bitter sea water in for him instead.
sentences.n: fest with schlafen is “fast, soundly.” The two halves mirror each other, gossen … aus against gossen … hinein, with “ihm aber” fronted to mark the switch: for him, on the other hand. einmal here is little more than “at some point.”

sentences.t: Als sie nun daheim ankamen, brachte der jüngste dem kranken König seinen Becher, damit er daraus trinken und gesund werden sollte.
sentences.l: When they now arrived at home, the youngest brought the sick king his cup, so that he should drink from it and become well.
sentences.i: When they came home, the youngest brought the sick king his cup, that he might drink from it and grow well.
sentences.n: nun in narrative is a light “now, at this point.” daheim = at home. This damit, with its verb at the end of the clause, is “so that” — not the damit “with that” of the sentences above; the word order tells them apart.

sentences.t: Kaum aber hatte er ein wenig von dem bitteren Meerwasser getrunken, so ward er noch kränker als zuvor.
sentences.l: Hardly, however, had he drunk a little of the bitter sea-water, so he became yet sicker than before.
sentences.i: But scarcely had he drunk a little of the bitter sea water when he grew sicker than before.
sentences.n: “Kaum hatte er …, so …” = hardly had he … when; kaum stands first and pushes the verb ahead of the subject. ward is the old past of werden; kränker is the comparative of krank.

sentences.t: Und wie er darüber jammerte, kamen die beiden ältesten Söhne und klagten den jüngsten an er hätte ihn vergiften wollen, sie brächten ihm das rechte Wasser des Lebens, und reichten es ihm.
sentences.l: And as he lamented over it, the two eldest sons came and accused the youngest he had wanted to poison him, they were bringing him the right water of life, and handed it to him.
sentences.i: And while he was lamenting over it, the two eldest sons came and accused the youngest of trying to poison him: they were bringing him the true water of life, they said — and handed it to him.
sentences.n: anklagen, to accuse, is separable: klagten … an, and the charge follows with no “that” at all. hätte and brächten are reported speech in the subjunctive, which is how the tale holds the lie at arm’s length. recht here is “right, true, genuine.”

sentences.t: Kaum hatte er davon getrunken, so fühlte er seine Krankheit verschwinden, und ward stark und gesund wie in seinen jungen Tagen.
sentences.l: Hardly had he drunk of it, so he felt his sickness disappear, and became strong and well as in his young days.
sentences.i: Scarcely had he drunk of it when he felt his sickness vanish, and grew strong and well as in his young days.
sentences.n: The same “kaum … so” frame as before, turned now to the good. fühlen takes a bare infinitive as English does: felt his sickness vanish.

sentences.t: Danach giengen die beiden zu dem jüngsten, verspotteten ihn und sagten „du hast zwar das Wasser des Lebens gefunden, aber du hast die Mühe gehabt und wir den Lohn;
sentences.l: After that the two went to the youngest, mocked him and said “you have indeed found the water of life, but you have had the trouble and we the reward;
sentences.i: After that the two went to the youngest, mocked him and said: “you found the water of life, sure enough, but you have had the labour and we the reward;
sentences.n: zwar grants a point before aber overturns it: you found it, yes, but … Mühe is trouble, toil; Lohn is wages, the pay for it. The second half drops its verb — “und wir den Lohn” — as English can too.

sentences.t: du hättest klüger sein und die Augen aufbehalten sollen, wir haben dirs genommen während du auf dem Meere eingeschlafen warst, und übers Jahr da holt sich einer von uns die schöne Königstochter.
sentences.l: you should have been cleverer and kept the eyes open, we have taken it from you while you had fallen asleep on the sea, and over the year one of us fetches himself the beautiful king’s-daughter.
sentences.i: you should have been cleverer and kept your eyes open; we took it from you while you lay asleep on the sea, and a year from now one of us will fetch the beautiful king’s daughter for himself.
sentences.n: “hättest … sollen” is the double infinitive of a past modal: should have been. aufbehalten is to keep on, to keep open. dirs = dir es, the dative carrying the person robbed. “übers Jahr” = a year from now, when the year is round. “sich holen” has a dative reflexive: to fetch for oneself.

sentences.t: Aber hüte dich daß du nichts davon verräthst, der Vater glaubt dir doch nicht, und wenn du ein einziges Wort sagst, so sollst du noch obendrein dein Leben verlieren, schweigst du aber, so soll dirs geschenkt sein.“
sentences.l: But guard yourself that you betray nothing of it, the father does not believe you anyway, and if you say a single word, then you shall lose your life on top of it, but keep you silent, then it shall be given you.”
sentences.i: But be on your guard that you betray nothing of it: our father will not believe you in any case, and if you say a single word you shall lose your life into the bargain; but if you keep silent, your life shall be a gift to you.”
sentences.n: verrathen (modern verraten) is to betray, to give away. doch concedes what both know: he will not believe you anyhow. obendrein = on top of that, into the bargain. “schweigst du aber” is another conditional with the verb first and no wenn. dirs = dir es, and “geschenkt sein” is to be granted as a gift — here, life spared.

sentences.t: Der alte König war zornig über seinen jüngsten Sohn und glaubte er hätte ihm nach dem Leben getrachtet.
sentences.l: The old king was angry over his youngest son and believed he had striven after his life.
sentences.i: The old king was angry with his youngest son, and believed that he had sought his life.
sentences.n: “zornig über” = angry at, about. “jemandem nach dem Leben trachten” is a fixed phrase, to seek someone’s life, to plot his death, the person in the dative: ihm. hätte is the subjunctive of what the king believed rather than of what was so.

sentences.t: Also ließ er den Hof versammeln und das Urtheil über ihn sprechen daß er heimlich sollte erschossen werden.
sentences.l: So he had the court assembled and the judgment spoken over him, that he should secretly be shot.
sentences.i: So he had the court assembled and judgment pronounced on him, that he should be secretly shot.
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive is the causative: to have a thing done. “das Urtheil sprechen” is the set phrase for pronouncing sentence; Urtheil is the 1857 spelling of Urteil. erschießen is to shoot dead.

sentences.t: Als der Prinz nun einmal auf die Jagd ritt und nichts Böses vermuthete, mußte des Königs Jäger mitgehen.
sentences.l: When the prince now one time rode out to the hunt and suspected nothing evil, the king’s huntsman had to go along.
sentences.i: One day, when the prince rode out to the hunt and suspected no harm, the king’s huntsman had to go with him.
sentences.n: “auf die Jagd reiten” = to ride out hunting. “nichts Böses” is an adjective used as a noun: nothing evil. “des Königs Jäger” puts the genitive first, older and weightier than “der Jäger des Königs.” vermuthete is the 1857 spelling of vermutete.

sentences.t: Draußen, als sie ganz allein im Wald waren, und der Jäger so traurig aussah, sagte der Prinz zu ihm „lieber Jäger, was fehlt dir?“
sentences.l: Outside, when they were quite alone in the wood, and the huntsman looked so sad, the prince said to him “dear huntsman, what is lacking to you?”
sentences.i: Out there, when they were quite alone in the wood and the huntsman looked so sad, the prince said to him: “dear huntsman, what ails you?”
sentences.n: “was fehlt dir?” is the ordinary way of asking what is wrong — literally what is wanting to you, the person in the dative. aussehen, to look, to appear, is separable: sah … aus.

sentences.t: Der Jäger sprach „ich kanns nicht sagen und soll es doch.“
sentences.l: The huntsman spoke “I cannot say it and yet am to.”
sentences.i: The huntsman said: “I cannot say it, and yet I must.”
sentences.n: kanns = kann es. sollen is the verb of what one is bound or told to do; left at the end with doch it means “and yet I am supposed to.” German drops the infinitive where English keeps a “to.”

sentences.t: Da sprach der Prinz „sage heraus was es ist, ich will dirs verzeihen.“
sentences.l: Then the prince spoke “say out what it is, I will forgive you it.”
sentences.i: Then the prince said: “speak out what it is; I will forgive you for it.”
sentences.n: “heraus sagen” = to say out, to come out with a thing; the 1857 text prints the two words apart. verzeihen takes the dative of the person and the accusative of the thing: dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte der Jäger, „ich soll euch todtschießen, der König hat mirs befohlen.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the huntsman, “I am to shoot you dead, the king has commanded it to me.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the huntsman, “I am to shoot you dead; the king has ordered me to.”
sentences.n: The huntsman says euch to the prince — the respectful plural of the tales, addressed to one man. todtschießen (modern totschießen) is to shoot dead. mirs = mir es; befehlen takes the dative of the person commanded.

sentences.t: Da erschrack der Prinz, und sprach „lieber Jäger, laß mich leben, da geb ich dir mein königliches Kleid, gib mir dafür dein schlechtes.“
sentences.l: Then the prince took fright, and spoke “dear huntsman, let me live, then I give you my royal garment, give me for it your poor one.”
sentences.i: Then the prince took fright and said: “dear huntsman, let me live; I will give you my royal clothes, and you give me your poor ones for them.”
sentences.n: erschrack is the old past of erschrecken (modern erschrak). laß and gib are du-imperatives in their bare old forms; geb is the clipped gebe. schlecht here has its older sense, plain, poor in quality, rather than morally bad. Kleid is any garment, not only a woman’s dress.

sentences.t: Der Jäger sagte „das will ich gerne thun, ich hätte doch nicht nach euch schießen können.“
sentences.l: The huntsman said “that I will gladly do, I could not have shot at you anyway.”
sentences.i: The huntsman said: “that I will gladly do; I could never have brought myself to shoot at you.”
sentences.n: “nach jemandem schießen” = to shoot at someone. “hätte … schießen können” is the double infinitive again: could have shot. doch here shrugs the order away: in any case, whatever I was told.

sentences.t: Da tauschten sie die Kleider, und der Jäger gieng heim, der Prinz aber gieng weiter in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: Then they exchanged the clothes, and the huntsman went home, but the prince went further in, into the wood.
sentences.i: Then they exchanged clothes, and the huntsman went home, while the prince went deeper into the wood.
sentences.n: tauschen is to swap, to exchange. “in den Wald hinein” doubles the direction, in … in, with hinein at the end marking movement away from the speaker; English gets it with “deeper into.”

sentences.t: Über eine Zeit, da kamen zu dem alten König drei Wagen mit Gold und Edelsteinen für seinen jüngsten Sohn: sie waren aber von den drei Königen geschickt, die mit des Prinzen Schwert die Feinde geschlagen und mit seinem Brot ihr Land ernährt hatten, und die sich dankbar bezeigen wollten.
sentences.l: After a time, there came to the old king three wagons with gold and precious stones for his youngest son: they were sent, however, by the three kings who with the prince’s sword had beaten the enemies and with his bread had fed their land, and who wanted to show themselves grateful.
sentences.i: After a time there came to the old king three wagons of gold and precious stones for his youngest son; but they were sent by the three kings who had beaten their enemies with the prince’s sword and fed their land with his bread, and who wished to show themselves grateful.
sentences.n: “über eine Zeit” = after a while. The da that follows a fronted phrase is a resumptive “then, there,” which English leaves out. “des Prinzen Schwert” again sets the genitive first. “sich dankbar bezeigen” = to show oneself thankful.

sentences.t: Da dachte der alte König „sollte mein Sohn unschuldig gewesen sein?“ und sprach zu seinen Leuten „wäre er noch am Leben, wie thut mirs so leid, daß ich ihn habe tödten lassen.“
sentences.l: Then the old king thought “should my son have been innocent?” and spoke to his people “were he still alive, how it grieves me that I have had him killed.”
sentences.i: Then the old king thought: “could my son have been innocent?” and said to his people: “if he were still alive — how it grieves me that I had him killed.”
sentences.n: sollte in a question is the verb of a dawning suspicion: can it be that …? “wäre er noch am Leben” is a wish with the verb first and no wenn. “es thut mir leid” = I am sorry, it grieves me, the person in the dative; mirs = mir es. “habe tödten lassen” is the double infinitive of the causative: had him killed.

sentences.t: „Er lebt noch,“ sprach der Jäger, „ich konnte es nicht übers Herz bringen euern Befehl auszuführen,“ und sagte dem König wie es zugegangen war.
sentences.l: “He is still alive,” spoke the huntsman, “I could not bring it over my heart to carry out your command,” and told the king how it had gone.
sentences.i: “He is still alive,” said the huntsman; “I could not bring myself to carry out your command” — and told the king how it had come about.
sentences.n: “es nicht übers Herz bringen” is fixed: not to be able to bring oneself to a thing. ausführen is separable, and with zu the particle takes it inside: auszuführen. euern is the older spelling of euren; the huntsman says ihr to the king. “zugehen” of an event is to come about, to happen.

sentences.t: Da fiel dem König ein Stein von dem Herzen, und er ließ in allen Reichen verkündigen, sein Sohn dürfte wiederkommen und sollte in Gnaden aufgenommen werden.
sentences.l: Then a stone fell from the king’s heart, and he had it proclaimed in all kingdoms, his son might come back and should be received in grace.
sentences.i: Then a stone fell from the king’s heart, and he had it proclaimed throughout all the kingdoms that his son might come back and should be received in favour.
sentences.n: “jemandem fällt ein Stein vom Herzen” is the same picture English has in “a weight off his heart,” the person in the dative: dem König. verkündigen is to proclaim. dürfte and sollte are reported speech again. “in Gnaden aufnehmen” is the formal language of a court pardon.

sentences.t: Die Königstochter aber ließ eine Straße vor ihrem Schloß machen, die war ganz golden und glänzend,
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter, however, had a road made before her castle, it was quite golden and gleaming,
sentences.i: But the king’s daughter had a road made before her castle, all golden and gleaming,
sentences.n: “machen lassen” is the causative: to have a thing made. Straße here is a made road, a highway, not a town street. Once more the relative die is carried on as a demonstrative — “that one was golden” — and the sentence runs straight on.

sentences.t: und sagte ihren Leuten wer darauf geradeswegs zu ihr geritten käme, das wäre der rechte, und den sollten sie einlassen, wer aber daneben käme, der wäre der rechte nicht, und den sollten sie auch nicht einlassen.
sentences.l: and said to her people whoever came riding on it straight to her, that was the right one, and him they should let in, but whoever came beside it, that one was not the right one, and him they should not let in either.
sentences.i: and told her people that whoever came riding straight up it to her, that was the right one, and him they should let in; but whoever came alongside it, that was not the right one, and him they should not let in.
sentences.n: wer … der is the old correlative pair, whoever … he. geradeswegs = straight, directly. daneben = beside it, alongside. käme, wäre and sollten are all reported speech in the subjunctive. einlassen, to let in, is separable.

sentences.t: Als nun die Zeit bald herum war, dachte der älteste er wollte sich eilen, zur Königstochter gehen und sich für ihren Erlöser ausgeben, da bekäme er sie zur Gemahlin und das Reich daneben.
sentences.l: When now the time was nearly round, the eldest thought he would hurry himself, go to the king’s daughter and give himself out for her deliverer, then he would get her for a wife and the kingdom besides.
sentences.i: When the year was nearly round, the eldest thought he would make haste, go to the king’s daughter and pass himself off as her deliverer; then he would get her to wife and the kingdom with her.
sentences.n: “herum sein” of a span of time is to be up, to be over. “sich ausgeben für” = to pass oneself off as. Erlöser is the one who breaks the spell, the deliverer. “zur Gemahlin bekommen” = to get as wife, Gemahlin being the courtly word. daneben here means “besides, into the bargain,” though the same word meant “alongside” a few lines earlier; the tale uses it in both senses.

sentences.t: Also ritt er fort, und als er vor das Schloß kam und die schöne goldene Straße sah, dachte er „das wäre jammerschade, wenn du darauf rittest,“ lenkte ab und ritt rechts nebenher.
sentences.l: So he rode away, and when he came before the castle and saw the fine golden road, he thought “that would be a crying shame, if you rode on it,” turned aside and rode alongside on the right.
sentences.i: So he rode off; and when he came before the castle and saw the fine golden road, he thought: “it would be a crying shame to ride on it” — turned aside, and rode alongside to the right.
sentences.n: jammerschade is a crying shame, made of Jammer, misery, and schade, a pity. He says du to himself, as one does in a private thought; rittest is the subjunctive of reiten. ablenken, to turn aside, is separable: lenkte … ab. nebenher = alongside.

sentences.t: Wie er aber vor das Thor kam, sagten die Leute zu ihm er wäre der rechte nicht, er sollte wieder fortgehen.
sentences.l: But when he came before the gate, the people said to him he was not the right one, he should go away again.
sentences.i: But when he came before the gate, the people told him that he was not the right one, and that he should go away again.
sentences.n: wie again for “when.” “der rechte nicht” leaves the negative at the end, where German likes it and English puts it early.

sentences.t: Bald darauf machte sich der zweite Prinz auf, und wie der zur goldenen Straße kam, und das Pferd den einen Fuß darauf gesetzt hatte, dachte er „es wäre jammerschade, das könnte etwas abtreten,“ lenkte ab und ritt links nebenher.
sentences.l: Soon after that the second prince set himself out, and when that one came to the golden road, and the horse had set the one foot on it, he thought “it would be a crying shame, that could tread something off,” turned aside and rode alongside on the left.
sentences.i: Soon after, the second prince set out; and when he came to the golden road, and his horse had set one foot on it, he thought: “it would be a crying shame, that might wear something away” — turned aside, and rode alongside to the left.
sentences.n: der standing alone is the demonstrative “that one,” pointing at the second prince. abtreten is to wear away or scrape off by treading; the subject of “das könnte etwas abtreten” is left vague — the treading, or the hoof doing it — and the English keeps it vague rather than choosing. The two elder brothers get the same words and the same fate, one to the right and one to the left.

sentences.t: Wie er aber vor das Thor kam, sagten die Leute er wäre der rechte nicht, er sollte wieder fortgehen.
sentences.l: But when he came before the gate, the people said he was not the right one, he should go away again.
sentences.n: The sentence repeats the elder brother’s almost exactly, only dropping “zu ihm”; the tales tell the second round in the words of the first.

sentences.t: Als nun das Jahr ganz herum war, wollte der dritte aus dem Wald fort zu seiner Liebsten reiten und bei ihr sein Leid vergessen.
sentences.l: When now the year was quite round, the third wanted to ride away out of the wood to his dearest and to forget his sorrow with her.
sentences.i: When the year was quite up, the third wished to ride out of the wood to his beloved, and to forget his sorrow with her.
sentences.n: Liebste is the beloved, the sweetheart — the superlative of lieb used as a noun. “fort … reiten” wraps the whole direction round the infinitive at the end. Leid is grief, sorrow, the harm done to him.

sentences.t: Also machte er sich auf, und dachte immer an sie und wäre gerne schon bei ihr gewesen, und sah die goldene Straße gar nicht.
sentences.l: So he set himself out, and thought always of her and would gladly have been with her already, and did not see the golden road at all.
sentences.i: So he set out, thinking always of her, and would gladly have been with her already; and he never saw the golden road at all.
sentences.n: “denken an” takes the accusative for what one thinks of. “wäre gerne … gewesen” is the subjunctive of a wish: he would gladly have been there. “gar nicht” = not at all.

sentences.t: Da ritt sein Pferd mitten darüber hin, und als er vor das Thor kam, ward es aufgethan, und die Königstochter empfieng ihn mit Freuden und sagte er wär ihr Erlöser und der Herr des Königreichs, und ward die Hochzeit gehalten mit großer Glückseligkeit.
sentences.l: Then his horse rode right over the middle of it, and when he came before the gate, it was opened, and the king’s-daughter received him with joy and said he was her deliverer and the lord of the kingdom, and the wedding was held with great happiness.
sentences.i: So his horse rode straight over the middle of it; and when he came before the gate it was opened, and the king’s daughter received him with joy and said that he was her deliverer and the lord of the kingdom; and the wedding was held with great rejoicing.
sentences.n: “mitten darüber hin” piles up three small words of place: right across the middle of it. aufgethan is the participle of aufthun (modern auftun), to open; empfieng is the 1857 spelling of empfing. wär is the clipped wäre, reported speech again. The last clause opens with its verb and lets the subject follow after it: “und ward die Hochzeit gehalten.”

sentences.t: Und als sie vorbei war, erzählte sie ihm daß sein Vater ihn zu sich entboten und ihm verziehen hätte.
sentences.l: And when it was past, she told him that his father had summoned him to himself and had forgiven him.
sentences.i: And when it was over, she told him that his father had summoned him to come, and had forgiven him.
sentences.n: entbieten is the old formal verb for sending word to someone, summoning him. verziehen is the participle of verzeihen, to forgive, which takes the dative of the person: ihm. hätte is once more the subjunctive of what she reports.

sentences.t: Da ritt er hin und sagte ihm alles, wie seine Brüder ihn betrogen und er doch dazu geschwiegen hätte.
sentences.l: Then he rode thither and told him everything, how his brothers had deceived him and he had yet kept silent to it.
sentences.i: Then he rode there and told him everything: how his brothers had betrayed him, and how he had kept silent about it all the same.
sentences.n: hinreiten is to ride there, away from the speaker, the prefix hin standing at the end. “dazu schweigen” = to hold one’s peace about a thing. geschwiegen is the participle of schweigen.

sentences.t: Der alte König wollte sie strafen, aber sie hatten sich aufs Meer gesetzt und waren fortgeschifft und kamen ihr Lebtag nicht wieder.
sentences.l: The old king wanted to punish them, but they had set themselves on the sea and had shipped away and did not come back their life-day.
sentences.i: The old king wished to punish them, but they had put out to sea and sailed away, and never came back as long as they lived.
sentences.n: “sich aufs Meer setzen” = to put to sea, as “sich auf ein Schiff setzen” was to go aboard. fortschiffen is to sail away. “ihr Lebtag” is a bare accusative of duration, for their lifetime; with nicht it means never again while they lived. The tale ends without a word of judgment on them.

glossary.all: all — used up, at an end (‘all werden’, of a stock running out; not the ordinary all/alle)
glossary.anhielt: anhalten — stopped, brought to a halt (3rd sg. past; separable: hielt … an)
glossary.ausgezogen: ausziehen — set out, marched off (past participle; separable)
glossary.auskunft: die Auskunft — information, directions (what one is told in answer)
glossary.ausziehen: ausziehen — to set out, to march out (separable; of soldiers and of sons leaving home)
glossary.auszuziehen: ausziehen — to set out, to march out (zu-infinitive, with zu inside: aus-zu-ziehen)
glossary.erbe: erben — (I) inherit (1st sg. present; not das Erbe, the inheritance)
glossary.geschickt: schicken — sent (past participle; not the adjective geschickt, skilful)
glossary.holt: holen — fetches (3rd sg. present; ‘sich etwas holen’ = to fetch for oneself)
glossary.kleid: das Kleid — garment, robe (any article of clothing, not only a woman’s dress)
glossary.kranken: krank — sick, ill (adjective, inflected: zum kranken König)
glossary.lenkte: lenken — turned, steered (3rd sg. past; here ablenken, separable: lenkte … ab, turned aside)
glossary.rede: die Rede — speech, talk (‘Rede und Antwort geben’ = to give a proper answer)
glossary.reichen: das Reich — kingdoms, realms (dat. pl.; in allen Reichen)
glossary.sage: sagen — say (du-imperative; ‘sage heraus’ = say out, come out with it)
glossary.schlag: schlagen — strike (du-imperative in the bare old form; ‘anschlagen an’ = to strike against)
glossary.trinkt: trinken — drinks (3rd sg. present; ‘davon trinken’ = to drink of it)
glossary.verderben: verderben — to perish, to be ruined; transitively, to ruin, to do for someone (verb)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. present; not weiß, white)
